The Sixth Circuit weighs whether the public has a First Amendment right to review secret Michigan courtroom audio after a judge's alleged verbal abuse.
Evidence: Court Filings, Oral Arguments, Washington Examiner Report 🌐
#Aletheia #Law

Litigants argue that withholding audio recordings of court proceedings where a judge allegedly abused a defendant violates constitutional transparency and public accountability.

Federal appeals judges are actively grappling with the constitutional tension between traditional state court privacy rules and First Amendment public access.
Resulting Judgement: (+0.70, +0.50) — Greater Good

Judicial review is actively testing institutional boundaries to determine whether public access extends to courtroom audio records.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit heard arguments in a lawsuit seeking to compel an Oakland County, Michigan, court to release audio from a contentious hearing.

Actual Article Body:
A federal appeals court grappled on Wednesday with whether to revive a lawsuit seeking to release Michigan courtroom audio from a hearing in which a judge allegedly verbally abused a defendant, after the state court only released a transcript of the proceeding.

A three-judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit heard arguments in the case brought by Samantha Hallman, who claims her brother was verbally abused by a judge during a plea hearing, over whether the Oakland County, Michigan, court should have to release the audio of the proceeding. Hallman claims in a filing to the appeals court that the judge overseeing the proceedings “lost her temper, refused to allow Mr. Hallman a promised opportunity to explain his conduct, and engaged in other ‘extremely unfair and intemperate conduct.'” Hallman wanted the recording to be published to “encourage voters to elect a better-qualified judge” and argued that the state court’s rule blocking the recording violates the First Amendment.
